summary: Defines an abstract architecture for Direct Data Placement and Remote Direct Memory Access protocols that run over Internet transports. It is a descriptive tool for understanding the protocols, not necessarily how to implement them. DDP places data into the right buffers, and RDMA lets peers access memory directly. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally data is copied several times before it lands where it belongs. This design lets it be dropped straight into the right spot in another computer's memory.

questions: how does rdma reduce data copies
subtitle: How to let remote computers access memory directly over Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: High-speed data transfers require many copies of data as it moves between the network interface, kernel buffers, and application buffers, consuming precious memory bandwidth and CPU cycles.
tldr.mechanism: Direct Data Placement (DDP) steers incoming data directly into application-specified buffers using steering tags, and Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) adds the ability for one peer to read or write another peer's memory buffers directly, both over standard Internet protocols.
tldr.outcome: Applications on high-bandwidth networks can achieve lower latency and higher throughput by avoiding intermediate data copies. This architecture works on any Internet transport (TCP, SCTP, DCCP) and is transport-independent, though best suited to reliable, ordered point-to-point connections.

today: RFC 4296 is an Informational document that defines the abstract architecture. It has not been obsoleted or updated. This architecture has been implemented in concrete protocols (RDMACM, iWARP, SoftRoCE) that run RDMA over TCP, DCCP, or Ethernet.

sections.title: An Architecture for Copy-Free Data Transfer
sections.content:
RFC 4296 defines an abstract architecture for Direct Data Placement (DDP) and Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) protocols that run over Internet transports. This architecture is a descriptive tool for understanding these protocols; it does not necessarily describe the correct way to implement them.

The central goal of DDP is to allow efficient placement of data into buffers designated by upper-layer protocols (such as RDMA). DDP does this by having the sender attach placement information to data packets, allowing the receiver's network interface to steer the data directly to its final destination without intermediate copies. The goal of RDMA is to provide semantics for Remote Direct Memory Access between peers: the ability for one computer to read from or write to another computer's memory buffers with authorization.

DDP and RDMA are transport-independent. They work on top of any Internet transport layer (SCTP, DCCP, framed TCP) and do not change the fundamental characteristics of the underlying transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a postal service that can deliver mail directly into specific drawers of your desk, and where you can reach into your friend's desk across town and grab what you need. That is what this architecture does with computer data.

sections.title: The DDP Protocol Layer
sections.content:
The DDP layer sits between an upper-layer protocol (like RDMA or an application protocol) and the transport (TCP, SCTP, or similar). At its core, DDP manages buffers—addressable collections of octets with a start address, an end address, and a set() method to write data.

A DDP message can be tagged (sent with placement information identifying a specific buffer and offset) or untagged (sent without placement information; the receiver posts buffers to receive them). A Steering Tag (stag_t) identifies the destination buffer, and an offset specifies where in the buffer the data should land. The sender supplements data with this DDP address information and sends it via the transport.

The DDP layer provides operations like ddp_send() for untagged messages, ddp_send_ddp() for tagged placement, ddp_register() to register a buffer, and ddp_recv() to retrieve incoming messages and reception indications. DDP messages may be split across multiple transport messages; the final fragment carries a notify flag and message ID to signal completion.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP is like a mailing label on a package. It says 'put this in drawer 3, starting at position 100' so the receiving computer knows exactly where to put the data without asking.

sections.title: The RDMA Protocol Layer
sections.content:
RDMA extends DDP by adding two primary capabilities. First, it adds RDMA Read, which allows one peer to read from buffers registered on a remote peer without the remote peer's involvement (though the remote peer may need to authenticate the request). This enables arbitrary, bidirectional data movement. When implemented in hardware, RDMA Read can be performed without involving the remote CPU at all.

Second, RDMA adds an untagged message service called Send, optimized for efficient hardware implementation. RDMA is layered as a client protocol on top of DDP. While DDP handles the placement of data into buffers, RDMA adds control semantics: operations like rdma_send() (send an untagged message), rdma_write() (place data to a tagged remote buffer), and rdma_read() (read from a tagged remote buffer).

RDMA buffers extend DDP buffers with a get() operation that retrieves a value, enabling remote read access. Buffer registration modes (permissions) control whether a registered buffer can be read, written, or both. Completions signal when an operation has finished, allowing applications to know when data is safe to use.
sections.plainLanguage: RDMA adds two tricks to DDP. One: you can reach into someone else's memory and pull out data without them having to send it. Two: there is a special fast way to send untagged messages that hardware can do very efficiently.

sections.title: Transport Independence and Constraints
sections.content:
DDP and RDMA are designed to work on transports with different characteristics: reliable or unreliable, ordered or unordered, single-source or multi-source, and single-destination or multi-destination (multicast).

However, the characteristics of the underlying transport directly affect the service provided. An unreliable or unordered transport will produce an unreliable or unordered RDMA service. Some RDMA features—particularly Send flow control and RDMA Read—translate poorly to unreliable or multipoint transports due to the complexity of managing endpoint state.

Buffer access must be consistent across multiple IP addresses on transports that support multi-homing (like SCTP). The Steering Tag must address the same buffer across all addresses within an association. For multidestination transports, all receivers must produce the same buffer address when registering a destination buffer. In practice, many RDMA applications depend on capabilities only available on point-to-point, reliable transports.
sections.plainLanguage: DDP works on any kind of network, but some networks are simpler than others. A fast, reliable, direct connection between two computers is the sweet spot. Trying it over an unreliable or broadcast network is possible but messy.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
DDP and RDMA themselves should not introduce new vulnerabilities beyond those of the transport. However, they must allow strict upper layers to prevent new vulnerabilities. Implementations must ensure that only explicitly supplied (registered) resources can be manipulated by DDP or RDMA messages.

A Steering Tag exports access to a buffer, so a critical aspect of security is controlling the scope of this access. It must be possible to individually control whether a Steering Tag permits remote read, remote write, or both, and these controls must be enforced on the endpoint (socket) where it was registered.

DDP and RDMA must protect against buffer reuse, buffer overflow, and integrity violations even from trusted but compromised peers. The recipient must be able to explicitly control peer access to buffer regions. Peer connections must pass authentication and authorization checks before beginning RDMA operations, and all peer accesses to buffers must be authenticated and authorized in the context of the connection. IPsec, applied on a packet-by-packet basis, is identified as a natural fit for securing RDMA, as it allows security processing before data placement occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: The big security challenge is making sure a malicious peer cannot read or write your memory without permission. You must be able to say 'you can read buffer A but not write it, and you cannot touch buffer B at all.'
